## A fixed multiplier gives an exponential model {#ss8-models .growth-lesson .growth-models}

::: {.split .growth-model-layout}
::: {.column-block}
<h3>Amount after <span data-math="n">n</span> periods</h3>

$$A_n=A_0\textcolor{#3b66a8}{R}^{\,n}$$

$A_0$ is the initial amount, at time $0$.

$R>1$: exponential growth.

$0<R<1$: exponential decay.
:::
::: {.column-block}
<h3>Compound interest</h3>

$$A=P\textcolor{#3b66a8}{(1+r)}^{\,n}$$

$P$ is the initial principal.

$r$ is the interest rate **per period**, written as a decimal.

Here, $R=1+r$.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}

The rate and the number of periods must use the **same time interval**.

:::

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet pp. 47, 50 · Exponential models</p>

::: notes

The amount starts at time zero, so n elapsed periods require n multiplications: A_0, A_0R, A_0R², …, A_0R^n. This explains the exponent n, compared with n−1 when the first amount is labelled term 1. Assume a positive initial amount for the growth/decay classifications. R=1 gives a constant amount. R is the multiplier on this slide; r in the compound-interest formula is the decimal interest rate, not the common ratio. The booklet uses r for a common ratio in later problems, so read its meaning from context. First click emphasises matching periods. In Example 8.1 students will convert a nominal annual rate to a monthly rate and count twelve months. Compound interest earned is A−P. No derivation is needed here.

:::
